title: ASSIGNMENT – 1
subtitle: Software Engineering (UCS3504) — Hospital Management System: Comprehensive Analysis, SDLC, SRS, Use Case and DFD
name: Srikrishna O S

sections.heading: AIM
sections.paragraph: To apply software engineering principles to analyze, model, and design a real-world software system. The chosen system is a Hospital Management System (HMS). This report presents a comprehensive study including problem definition, scope, objectives, risk analysis, ethics and sustainability, SDLC selection and schedule, feasibility study, requirements engineering with a full IEEE-style SRS, use case modeling with detailed scenarios, and data-flow design with a data dictionary.

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION AND PROBLEM DEFINITION
sections.paragraph: Modern hospitals operate in a high-pressure environment where accurate, real-time information can be the difference between efficient patient care and operational chaos. Many hospitals still rely on a mix of paper files, spreadsheets, and disconnected departmental applications. This fragmentation causes delayed appointments, duplicated tests, prescription errors, billing disputes, and poor resource utilization. The proposed Hospital Management System (HMS) is a unified, web-based platform that integrates patient registration, appointment scheduling, electronic medical records (EMR), diagnosis, prescriptions, pharmacy, laboratory, billing, admission/discharge, staff scheduling, inventory, and analytics.
bullets: Target users: Patients, doctors, nurses, receptionists, pharmacists, lab technicians, billing staff, and hospital administrators.
Primary stakeholders: Hospital management, clinical staff, patients and their families, insurance companies, pharmacy suppliers, medical device vendors, and government health authorities.
Project scope: A multi-tenant, role-based web application supporting outpatient and inpatient workflows for a 250-bed multi-specialty hospital.
Major modules: Patient Registration, Appointment Scheduling, EMR, Doctor Workbench, Pharmacy & Inventory, Laboratory, Billing & Payments, Admission/Discharge, Staff Scheduling, Reports & Analytics.
Expected outcomes: Reduced average waiting time by 40%, elimination of duplicate records, faster billing cycles, centralized audit-ready data, and improved regulatory compliance.

sections.heading: 2. ETHICS, LEGAL AND SUSTAINABILITY CONSIDERATIONS
sections.paragraph: Building an HMS involves sensitive personal health information. Ethical design must be baked into the system from the start, not added later.
bullets: Patient privacy and confidentiality: The system must comply with the Digital Information Security in Healthcare Act (DISHA) India and follow HIPAA-style principles for data minimization, consent, and breach notification.
Informed consent: Patients must explicitly consent to data sharing with insurers, researchers, or third-party providers; consent must be revocable.
Data minimization: Collect only the data needed for care, billing, or compliance; avoid unnecessary personal identifiers.
Fair access and digital inclusion: The UI should support local languages, high-contrast modes, and simple navigation so elderly and differently-abled users are not excluded.
Algorithmic transparency: Any decision-support or triage scoring must be explainable and auditable, with human oversight.
Sustainability: Cloud deployment reduces physical hardware and paper consumption, supporting SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure) and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production).
Professional responsibility: Developers, doctors, and administrators must follow ACM/IEEE code of ethics and not bypass safety checks for speed or profit.

sections.heading: 3. SDLC MODEL SELECTION
sections.paragraph: The Incremental Software Development Life Cycle model is selected for the HMS. A hospital cannot pause operations for a big-bang replacement. The Incremental model lets the team build and deploy the system in prioritized, working increments, collect real user feedback, and extend the product over time. Each increment delivers a usable subsystem, reducing both technical and business risk.

rows: Modules go live one at a time; old processes continue for unaffected departments
High-risk modules (e.g., EMR, billing) are prototyped and validated early
Doctors and staff can use real increments and request changes before later modules are built
Management can pause or reprioritize increments based on ROI
Each increment is validated independently, making audits easier
Working appointment portal and reception dashboard

sections.heading: 3.3 PROJECT SCHEDULE
sections.paragraph: The proposed schedule covers 20 weeks, with planning in the first month and each implementation increment taking approximately three weeks.

sections.heading: 4. FEASIBILITY ANALYSIS
sections.paragraph: A feasibility study evaluates whether the HMS project is worth pursuing. The analysis covers technical, economic, operational, legal, and schedule dimensions.

sections.heading: 4.1 TECHNICAL FEASIBILITY
sections.paragraph: The system can be built using mature open-source and commercial technologies. The recommended stack is Spring Boot or Django for the backend, React for the frontend, PostgreSQL for transactional data, Redis for caching, and AWS/Azure/ on-premise private cloud for hosting. HL7/FHIR libraries and DICOM viewers are available for integration with lab and imaging systems. The hospital already has LAN/WAN connectivity, so no major network upgrade is needed.

rows: Annual savings from reduced paper, faster billing, fewer duplicate tests

sections.heading: 4.3 OPERATIONAL FEASIBILITY
sections.paragraph: The hospital has an IT helpdesk and network infrastructure. Doctors and nurses are familiar with computers, but a structured change-management program is essential. Operational feasibility is high because the system mirrors existing workflows rather than forcing a complete redesign.

sections.heading: 4.4 LEGAL AND REGULATORY FEASIBILITY
sections.paragraph: The HMS must comply with the IT Act 2000, DISHA (India), and data-localization guidelines. With role-based access, encryption, audit logs, and consent management, compliance is achievable. A legal review of insurance and billing integration is recommended before go-live.

sections.heading: 4.5 SCHEDULE FEASIBILITY
sections.paragraph: A 20-week incremental plan with a working MVP after 8 weeks is realistic for a team of 6–8 developers. Buffer time is included for user acceptance testing and integration.

sections.heading: 5. REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING
sections.paragraph: Requirements engineering identifies what the HMS must do and how well it must do it. Functional requirements define behavior; non-functional requirements define quality attributes.

rows: The system shall register a new patient, generate a unique patient ID, and store demographics, contact, insurance, and emergency details.
The system shall allow patients or receptionists to search doctors by department and book, reschedule, or cancel appointments without double-booking.
The system shall let doctors view patient history, add diagnosis notes, prescribe medicines, and order lab tests.
The system shall dispatch prescriptions to the pharmacy and update the dispensing status.
The system shall generate consolidated bills from consultation, lab, pharmacy, and room charges, and support cash, card, UPI, and insurance payments.
The system shall manage admission, bed allocation, and discharge with discharge summaries.
The system shall maintain medicine and consumable inventory with stock alerts.
The system shall schedule doctors and nursing staff by department and shift.
The system shall provide dashboards and reports for administration.
The system shall notify patients and staff via SMS/email for appointments, reports, and bills.
Availability: 99.9% uptime during operating hours; critical modules must failover within 60 seconds.
Performance: Search and booking response time under 2 seconds for 95% of requests.
Security: AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit, RBAC, MFA for admins, and immutable audit logs.
Scalability: Support 100 concurrent users in phase 1 and 1,000 users by year 3.
Usability: Responsive UI, multi-language support, accessibility compliance (WCAG 2.1 Level AA).
Reliability: Daily automated backups, point-in-time recovery within 24 hours.
Maintainability: Modular architecture, test coverage above 80%, and CI/CD pipelines.

sections.paragraph: The use case diagram identifies the actors and the major functions they perform. Patients interact with registration and appointments; doctors with diagnosis and prescriptions; receptionists with admissions; pharmacists, lab staff, billing staff, and administrators with their respective modules.

sections.heading: 7. DATA FLOW MODEL
sections.paragraph: The Data Flow Diagram (DFD) shows how data moves between external entities, processes, and data stores. The Context DFD presents the HMS as a single process. The Level 1 DFD decomposes it into nine interacting processes with six data stores and the relevant external entities.

sections.heading: 8. TESTING AND QUALITY ASSURANCE
bullets: Unit testing: Each service and controller tested with JUnit/Mocha; target 80% code coverage.
Integration testing: Verify HL7/FHIR message flow between EMR, lab, and pharmacy modules.
System testing: End-to-end workflows including patient registration, appointment, consultation, billing, and discharge.
User acceptance testing: Doctors, nurses, and receptionists validate real-world scenarios in a staging environment.
Security testing: Penetration testing, RBAC verification, and audit-log completeness.

sections.heading: 9. ASSUMPTIONS AND DEPENDENCIES
bullets: The hospital will provide accurate master data (doctors, departments, room inventory, medicine catalog) before go-live.
Stable internet and LAN/WAN connectivity are available at all hospital locations.
Legacy paper records will be digitized for active patients only; historical records can be scanned on demand.
Insurance company APIs or file formats for claim submission are available.
Regulatory requirements (DISHA, IT Act) remain stable during development.

sections.heading: 10. CONCLUSION
sections.paragraph: The proposed Hospital Management System addresses the major operational pain points of a multi-specialty hospital through an integrated, incremental, and secure software solution. The analysis shows that the project is technically, economically, operationally, legally, and schedule-feasible. The Incremental SDLC model is appropriate because it allows the hospital to adopt modules gradually without disrupting daily operations. Use case and DFD models confirm that patient data flows cleanly through registration, appointment, consultation, pharmacy, lab, billing, and administration. With strong security, privacy, and sustainability practices, the HMS can improve patient care quality, reduce administrative overhead, and support regulatory compliance.
